title: GPU Fleet & Networking IaC + CI/CD Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document describes Redwood Inference's standard patterns, recommended Terraform modules, CI/CD pipelines, and runbooks for operating the GPU fleet and associated cloud accounts and networking. It is intended for infra engineers, SRE, and platform owners who onboard new regions, models, or capacity pools.

Goals
- Provide repeatable IaC patterns for GPU instance pools and VPC/networking that support Dedicated and Private deployments.
- Standardize CI/CD for module releases, infra changes, and capacity rollouts.
- Document runbooks for common GPU/network incidents and capacity management procedures.
- Define ownership, SLOs, and escalation paths.

Scope
- GPU fleet (A100/H100 instance pools, autoscaling policies, placement groups)
- Cloud accounts and networking (VPCs, subnets, route tables, NAT, peering, Transit Gateway)
- Terraform modules and registry usage (internal module registry)
- CI/CD for module tests, plans, and gated deploys (staging -> prod)
- Runbooks for degraded nodes, OOMs, network partitions, and scale events

Owners and Contacts
- Primary owner: infra-gpu-team (team channel: #infra-gpu)
- On-call: infra-oncall@redwood.com (pager escalation documented in oncall playbook)
- Module maintainer: modules-team@redwood.com

Key SLOs and Operational Thresholds
- GPU pool availability SLO: 99.95% (monthly) per-region per-pool.
- Node readiness (kubelet-ready / agent-connected): target 99.9% across fleet.
- Autoscaling responsiveness: scale-up 95th percentile < 90s for warm pools, < 300s for cold starts.
- Cost guardrail: per-pool average utilization target 40%-70%. Alert if > 80% or < 20% for 24h.

Architecture and Naming Conventions
- Account naming: redwood-<env>-gpu-<region> (e.g., redwood-prod-gpu-us-west-2)
- VPC: vpc-gpu-<region>-<suffix>
- Subnets: private-subnet-az{a,b,c}-gpu
- Instance pools (Terraform resource): gpu-instance-pool.<pool_name>
- Module naming in registry: github.com/redwood-inference/modules//gpu-instance-pool?ref=v1.2.0

Recommended Terraform Modules
- modules/networking-vpc: creates VPC, private/public subnets, route tables, NAT gateway config.
- modules/gpu-instance-pool: thin wrapper to create ASG/managed instance groups, instance profiles, boot scripts, GPU drivers, and node labels. Supports warm pools and gpu-preemptible (spot) variants.
- modules/iam-roles: IAM roles and instance profiles for fleet nodes and autoscaler.
- modules/monitoring-agent: deploys metrics/logging agent and required IAM policies.

Example module usage (recommended pattern)
```
module "vpc_gpu_usw2" {
  source = "github.com/redwood-inference/modules/networking-vpc?ref=v1.3.0"
  name   = "vpc-gpu-us-west-2"
  region = "us-west-2"
  cidr   = "10.40.0.0/16"
  private_subnets = ["10.40.1.0/24", "10.40.2.0/24", "10.40.3.0/24"]
}

module "gpu_pool_realtime" {
  source        = "github.com/redwood-inference/modules/gpu-instance-pool?ref=v2.0.0"
  name          = "realtime-a100-80gb"
  region        = "us-west-2"
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge" # replace with H100/A100 family per workload
  min_size      = 2
  max_size      = 200
  warm_pool     = true
  labels        = { role = "inference", pool = "realtime" }
}
```

Module Inputs / Requirements (summary table)
- modules/networking-vpc: name, region, cidr, private_subnets (list), public_subnets (optional), nat_gateway_count (int), enable_flow_logs (bool)
- modules/gpu-instance-pool: name, region, instance_type, ami_id or launch_template_id, min_size, max_size, warm_pool (bool), spot_policy, iam_role_arn
- modules/iam-roles: list of roles, managed_policies (list), assume_role_principals

Module testing and versioning
- All modules must include: unit tests (terratest), integration plan validation in ephemeral accounts, and example usage in examples/ directory.
- Semantic versioning required (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Breaking changes require a major bump + migration guide.
- Release process: module PR -> automated tests -> manual reviewer approval -> tag and publish to internal registry.

CI/CD and Build Patterns
- Repositories:
  - infra/modules (monorepo of modules)
  - infra/live (per-environment configurations - staging/prod)
  - infra/packer (AMI/driver builds)
  - infra/pipelines (shared pipeline templates)

- Pipeline stages (recommended):
  1. Terraform fmt & validate
  2. Unit tests (terratest / go test)
  3. Static checks (tfsec, checkov)
  4. Plan (with remote backend in ephemeral/test account)
  5. Manual approval for production apply (required for infra/live/prod)
  6. Apply (gated, with plan artifact and approve by infra-approvers group)

- Branching: trunk-based. Release branches only for emergency bugfixes.
- PR requirements: 2 approvers (at least one module owner), passing pipeline, change log entry when public API changes.
- Pipeline examples: CircleCI/Drone/GitHub Actions templates live in infra/pipelines/. Use reusable workflows to enforce step consistency.

Bootstrap and AMI build process
- Use Packer to build GPU node AMIs with drivers (NVIDIA driver, CUDA, NCCL) and baked agents. Image pipeline outputs launch_template_id for consumption by gpu-instance-pool module.
- Image tagging: redwood-gpu-<kernel>-<cuda>-<date>-vX
- Example packer command: packer build -var-file=us-west-2.pkrvars.hcl gpu-node.json

Runbooks (quick reference)
1) High-level GPU node degradation\- Symptoms: node flapping NotReady, kubelet OOM, agent disconnects.\- Initial checks:
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady
   - check node agent logs: journalctl -u redwood-agent -b
   - cloud console: instance status (status checks), CPU/GPU utilization
\- Remediation steps:
   1. If instance status checks failing, stop/start the instance in cloud console (non-destructive).
   2. If driver crash: cordon the node, drain workloads (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data), recreate AMI if recurring.
   3. Replace via autoscaler: reduce desired count then restore, or force terminate instance to trigger replacement.
   4. Post-incident: capture kernel/dmesg, nvdriver logs, and attach to incident ticket.

2) Network partition affecting GPU pools\- Symptoms: increased pod restarts, control-plane disconnects for a subset of nodes.\- Initial checks:
   - Verify VPC route tables and NACLs for recent changes.
   - Check Transit Gateway/Peering health (console + CloudWatch/Azure Monitor).
   - Verify Security Group rules, recent security group updates.
\- Remediation:
   1. If route table change caused issue: roll back route table change (Terraform revert) or attach alternate route.
   2. If NAT gateway failures: switch subnets to alternate NAT gateway or failover to reserved NAT.
   3. Open a change freeze and page network oncall (network-oncall@redwood.com).

3) Autoscaling not triggering (unexpected load surge)\- Symptoms: queue length grows, request latency increases, cold start penalties.\- Initial checks:
   - Check autoscaler metrics: scale recommendations, cooldown windows.
   - Verify CloudWatch/Stackdriver alarms for ASG scaling activities.
\- Remediation:
   1. Manually increase desired capacity for pool: terraform apply to bump max/desired in emergency branch.
   2. Toggle warm pool to on for the affected pool.
   3. If spot interruptions causing gaps: fallback to non-spot pool by enabling on-demand fallback policy.

Postmortem guidance
- For any incident that breaches SLO or leads to >1 hour degraded production: create incident ticket, assign primary/secondary, capture timeline, root cause, and follow-up actions. Use the incident template in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template.

Operational Playbook: Capacity Planning and Rollout Steps
1. Forecast demand (monthly) using model-owner inputs and historical throughput.
2. Calculate required GPU-hours and map to pool configurations (instance type, shards).
3. Open infra RFC: include cost estimate, failure modes, rollback plan, and security review.
4. Create feature branch in infra/live with new/updated module versions and staging config.
5. Run plan in staging account and exercise scale-up tests (synthetic load).
6. Schedule production deploy during low-traffic window, require 2 approvers and oncall present.
7. Monitor cost, utilization, and tail latency for 48h post-rollout.

Security and Compliance Notes
- Ensure node IAM roles follow least privilege. Avoid wildcard policies on node instance profiles.
- Flow logs enabled for all GPU VPCs (retention per security policy).
- Key material: use KMS for any secrets baked into AMIs. Use SOPS for Terraform variable files.

Appendix: Useful Commands and Queries
- List GPU pools: terraform state list | grep gpu-instance-pool
- Check node conditions: kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.status.conditions[?(@.type==\"Ready\")].status}{"\n"}{end}'
- View autoscaler recommendations (GKE/Cluster Autoscaler logs)
- Example emergency patch apply (one-line): git checkout -b emergency/scale-up && sed -i 's/max_size = 200/max_size = 400/' env/prod/gpu-pools.tf && git commit -am "emergency: scale up prod gpu pool" && gh pr create --title "Emergency scale up" --body "Emergency scale up due to latency" && gh pr merge --auto

References
- modules registry: internal modules registry (https://modules.redwood.internal)
- GPU capacity runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Infra CI templates: /confluence/eng-infra/team-wiki/infra-pipelines-templates
